newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German chemical groups slip despite records.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German chemical groups slip despite records.

text.p: Germany's two biggest chemical and drugs groups on Tuesday posted record 1996 profits but shares slumped as the market reacted with disappointment when widespread hopes of a higher dividend were not fulfilled.

Shares in Hoechst AG, Europe's largest chemicals group, plummeted about five percent to lead overall losers in afternoon trading after the group announced a near eight percent increase in its 1996 dividend to 1.40 marks.
But after talk circulated last week that Hoechst, standing to make large extraordinary profits from divestments, might double its dividend to 2.60 marks, the market scoffed at the payout.

Similarly shares in Bayer AG, traditionally the strongest and steadiest earner among Germany's three chemicals giants, fell more than two percent, even though the group set new records on profits and sales and raised its dividend by 13 percent.
Bayer shares traded at 75.27 marks after having been sharply higher on Monday.

"The market had expected surprises from the German chemical companies, people had fantasies that these groups would pay big bonus dividends, and now these are disappointed," said Peter Mackey, analyst at Kleinwort Benson in London.

Bayer reported its net profit surged 13.5 percent to 2.747 billion marks ($1.6 billion) with pre-tax profit rising 6.7 percent to 4.436 billion marks and sales jumping nine percent to 48.6 billion marks. The dividend was raised to 1.70 marks.
The numbers largely met analyst forecasts, but several said the market had become so spoiled by the performance of German chemical groups that even these results were not enough.

"When figures are in line with expectations, the share price drops on profit-taking. But when figures are below expectations, the share price is going to go down big time on profit-taking," a Frankfurt-based dealer said.
This was exactly what happened at Hoechst after the company said pre-tax profits surged 29 percent to a record 5.28 billion marks although sales slipped two percent to 50.9 billion marks.
Analysts said Hoechst's numbers, although strong on the surface, were actually disappointing as profit gains were driven by a 2.5 billion mark pre-tax gain generated by divestments last year.
These divestments were also responsible for the drop in sales, Hoechst said, adding that sales would have climbed one percent had it not been for the spin-offs.
The companies gave only a brief overview of results, saving detailed information for Hoechst's annual news conference on Wednesday and Bayer's next Tuesday.
BASF, the third firm making up Germany's chemical triumvirate, will release its core numbers on March 18 and hold its news conference on April 2.
Analysts had expected all companies to post strong results as they benefited not only from ongoing restructuring and cost-cutting but also more favourable currency exchange rates.

The groups' drugs divisions were expected to have done particularly well, helping to offset weaker performances in some bulk chemicals areas where higher raw materials prices and softer prices due raised costs.

Hoechst's ambitious restructuring plan, which envisions turning the company into a strategic management holding company, leaving individual business units as separate entities responsible for their performance, was approved by the supervisory board, Hoechst said.
As part of this plan, Hoechst said it planned to spin off its diagnostics division but would at first continue to run the business with a partner as a joint-venture.

Last December, Hoechst announced plans to spin off the specialty chemicals division to Swiss group Clariant AG, and now Hoechst board member Karl-Gerhard Seifert, head of that division, would leave the board to become chief executive officer at Clariant.
--Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525 ($ = 1.705 German Marks)
